item.title: Core Keeper Accessories — Necklaces, Rings and Polished Gear
item.description: Accessories are the jewelry and bag slots that sit outside your armor set: a Necklace, a Ring and a Backpack slot. They are where builds actually get defined — armor gives stats, accessories give thematic effects: minion builds, fishing-as-range-damage, explosive crits, mana-barrier tanking, and pet buffs all live in jewelry. Most are crafted at the Jewelry Workbench (Iron Workbench tier) or the upgraded Proficient Jewelry Workbench, with polished versions available on early and mid-tier pieces.

item.title: Core Keeper Achievements
item.description: Achievements in Core Keeper are the Steam trophy trackers that shadow your run: roughly sixty trophies split between boss kills, skill masteries, rare collectibles and a handful of deliberately silly hidden tasks. Many show their condition up front, while the hidden ones stay blank until you stumble into them. How the list is structured Visible trophies hand you the objective in the Steam client; hidden trophies show only a name and an icon, so spoilers are built into the design.

item.title: Core Keeper Armor Guide — Set Bonuses and Damage Reduction
item.description: Armor is the three-piece defensive layer you wear on your head, chest and legs. Each piece adds a flat armor score plus a small sprinkling of offensive stats — max health, % damage, critical chance, attack speed — and matching pieces from the same set unlock set bonuses at 2, 3 or (rarely) 5 pieces. The trap for new players is treating armor as a raw number: the real defense math caps the benefit, which means piling more and more armor past a soft plateau buys almost nothing.

item.title: Core Keeper Automation — Electricity, Wires and Auto Farms
item.description: Automation is the set of powered machines that turn a base into a self-running factory: drills chew through Ore Boulders while you are off fighting, conveyor belts ferry dropped loot into chests, and Robot Arms pull items between inventories so you never have to walk back. Every electrical machine runs on a simple two-wire logic — a power source, a length of conducting wire, and whatever you want switched on the other end.

item.title: Core Keeper Biomes — Inner, Outer and Sub-Biomes Explained
item.description: Source: Biomes — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg) and World — Core Keeper Wiki, cross-checked against this site’s biome data. Distances are approximate tile counts from The Core. Biomes are the geometrically defined colour-coded zones of a Core Keeper world, each with its own terrain, ores, enemy roster, fish catches and native bosses. The layout is radial and deterministic: the ring distances are the same on every world, but the angular position of each biome is randomised by the seed.

item.title: Core Keeper Boss Mechanics — Summoning, Scanners and Respawns
item.description: Bosses are the large signature enemies that gate progression and mark biomes. They spawn at fixed distances from The Core at random angles, which means you can triangulate them by how far you have walked rather than memorising a seed. Every boss falls into one of three buckets: story bosses that drop the hearts and souls you need to power The Core and open new biomes, optional side bosses that farm materials and legendary recipes, and post-game bosses that unlock after the main story ends.

item.title: Core Keeper Christmas Event — Festive Loot, Costumed Mobs and Presents
item.description: Source: Christmas Seasonal Event — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg). Drop rates and recipes below are taken directly from that page; where a number could not be verified it is marked 数据待核. The Christmas Seasonal Event is Core Keeper’s longest and richest celebration, running roughly Dec 14 – Jan 4 across the new year. While it is live, the world visibly transforms: The Core itself, boss statues and certain other objects become coated in a temporary snow layer that melts away again when the event ends.

item.title: Core Keeper Cooking
item.description: Cooking is how you turn raw foraged ingredients into dishes that punch far above their weight. Dropping two ingredients into a Cooking Pot produces a meal with stronger buffs, longer duration, and hidden stat combinations you’d never see from eating them raw. Understanding the hidden math behind the pot is what separates a good survivor from an endgame-ready one. How the Cooking Pot works Set a Cooking Pot down on any flat surface, walk up to it, and interact to open its interface.

item.title: Core Keeper Crafting Guide — Workbenches, Anvils and Stations
item.description: Crafting is how you turn raw ore, wood and drops into tools, armour, furniture and automation parts. Almost everything is made at a station you place in your base, although a handful of items can be crafted straight from your inventory. Stations form a long progression ladder: every new bench automatically carries over every recipe from the tier below, so you never have to rebuild an old recipe just because you unlocked a newer one.

item.title: Core Keeper Dungeons — Generated Structure Atlas by Biome
item.description: Source: World — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg), “Dungeon types (list)”. Map-appearance descriptions are qualitative; exact counts per seed vary. Beyond the plain terrain, every Core Keeper world is built from a repeating vocabulary of procedurally generated dungeons — networks of linked rooms that the generator stamps into a biome. Unlike the hand-placed set pieces covered on Scenes, these structure types recur in every world, just at different angles and mirrored or flipped layouts.

item.title: Core Keeper Easter Event — The Great Egg Hunt and Awakened Azeos
item.description: Source: The Great Egg Hunt — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg). Egg drops, recipes and Awakened Azeos numbers below are taken from that page; the event’s recurring window comes from this site’s verified Seasonal Events calendar. The Great Egg Hunt is Core Keeper’s Easter seasonal event — and the very first seasonal event the game ever ran, originally held April 13–19. It now recurs every spring, with a default window of roughly Apr 5 – Apr 16.

item.title: Core Keeper Fishing
item.description: Fishing is a leisure skill in Core Keeper that quietly pays for itself: toss a rod into any water tile, wait for a bite, and pull up fish, ore, kelp, loose tools or even locked chests. It also feeds the cooking loop, because a well-cooked fish dish hands you a real damage buff right before a boss attempt. How a catch actually works Stand next to any water source and cast the bobber.

item.title: Core Keeper Gardening
item.description: Gardening lets you turn loose seeds into a repeatable supply of food, fiber and crafting materials. You till a patch of suitable dirt, plant a seed, keep it watered, and pick the mature crop by hand. Nearly every harvest also feeds the cooking loop, so a well-kept farm is the backbone of long-term survivability in the underground caves. item.title: Core Keeper Halloween Event — Creepy Costume Party and Samhain
item.description: Source: this page is synthesised from this site’s own verified seasonal notes (Seasonal Events, Seasonal Workbenches, Seasonal Merchant). Note: atma.gg has no dedicated Halloween / Samhain article (the candidate URLs return 404), so exact drop tables and recipes below are intentionally omitted and marked 数据待核 rather than guessed. The Halloween Seasonal Event — called the Creepy Costume Party in-game, and Samhain in the wiki’s internal naming — runs roughly Oct 25 – Nov 7.

item.title: Core Keeper Map Structure — The Core, Distance Arcs and Fixed Landmarks
item.description: Source: World — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg), especially the “Set distance locations” and generation-algorithm sections. Distances are approximate tile counts from The Core. A Core Keeper map is a radial coordinate system, not a random blob. Everything important sits on a circle around The Core: only the angle is randomised by the seed, while the distance is fixed. Once you stop thinking “which direction?” and start thinking “which arc?”, finding bosses and legendary gear stops being blind digging.

item.title: Core Keeper Mechanics
item.description: Mechanics is the set of hidden formulas behind every number in Core Keeper: how your attacks scale, how much punishment your armour actually soaks, how power-ups wear off, and why bosses suddenly feel twice as scary with a friend online. Most players beat the early game by feel, but once you start min-maxing around Scarlet, Octarine and legendary gear, the order these bonuses apply decides whether a build is strong or merely okay.

item.title: Core Keeper Mining
item.description: Mining means breaking walls to dig out metal ore and other materials as you explore. Early on you chew through dirt, stone and ore veins by hand, but the real bottleneck is damage thresholds: every wall type absorbs a flat chunk of your mining power before your pickaxe starts actually chipping it. Once Drills unlock later, giant Ore Boulders become a far more efficient supply of metal — but until then, knowing which pickaxe to craft next is the single biggest speed-up available.

item.title: Core Keeper Progression Route — Boss Gates and Area Unlocks
item.description: Source: World — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg) and The Great Wall — Core Keeper Wiki, combined with this site’s boss and biome data. Exact summon-item names are 数据待核 against the current build. Core Keeper does not let you wander freely. Progress is gated in two locked ways: bosses act as doors to the next region, and The Great Wall is a hard wall until the inner-boss chain is done. This page lays out the intended route from The Core to the far endgame, so you know exactly which boss unlocks which area — and which travel tech to craft to keep up.

item.title: Core Keeper Scenes
item.description: Scenes are the hand-designed set pieces scattered across an otherwise procedural world. The tunnels, ores and dirt around you are generated algorithmically, but a shrine, a buried chest room, a merchant’s cell or a maze is a pre-built structure stamped into the map whole. Learning to recognize them by shape turns routine digging into targeted treasure hunting. What makes a scene different from terrain Most of the world is rolled on the fly, but scenes follow their own rules:

item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Events
item.description: Seasonal events are short, theme-driven celebrations that transform the underworld for a few weeks every year — pumpkins in autumn, snow and presents in winter, cherry blossoms in spring. During each window, certain enemies and bosses get a visual reskin, the main-menu logo changes to match the theme, and a roster of exclusive food, vanity and building items becomes available. Most of that limited loot is sold by the travelling Seasonal Merchant, so collecting the full set depends on logging in at the right time.

item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Merchant — How to Summon and What They Sell
item.description: The Seasonal Merchant is the travelling vendor who shows up only during real-world celebrations — Halloween, Christmas, Easter and the rest. They do not wander in on their own; you have to invite them with a specific crafting item. Their stock is event-exclusive and is bought with event-specific currency, not ordinary coins, so missing the window means waiting a full year for the same items to return. item.title: Core Keeper Seasonal Workbenches — Event-Only Crafting Stations
item.description: Each recurring celebration adds its own event-only workbench to the game. These benches are not part of the normal workbench ladder — they do not inherit recipes from the Copper/Tin/Iron tier, and they are not permanent unlocks. They exist only during their event window, are bought from the Seasonal Merchant, and vanish from the merchant’s stock when the celebration ends. Anything you have already crafted, however, stays in your storage forever.

item.title: Core Keeper Skills
item.description: Skills are your character’s passive progression track. Rather than spending points by hand, you earn experience simply by doing the activities the game already expects — swinging a pickaxe, swinging a sword, running around, planting seeds — and that experience slowly fills each skill bar toward level 100. Every discipline grants a small permanent bonus as it levels, and every fifth level hands you a talent point to spend in that skill’s own tree.

item.title: Core Keeper The Great Wall — The Outer Biome Gate
item.description: The Great Wall is an unbreakable, undulating ring of mechanical-looking blocks that separates the three inner biomes from the outer world. It is not a natural formation you can dig through — every tool, weapon and explosive bounces off it. It exists purely as a progression gate: until The Core lets you take it down, the Azeos’ Wilderness, the Sunken Sea and the Desert of Beginnings are off-limits no matter how far you walk.

item.title: Core Keeper Valentine Event — Love Letters, Gifts and the Crafting Table
item.description: Source: Valentine Seasonal Event — Core Keeper Wiki (atma.gg). Prices, recipes and drop rates below are taken directly from that page; the four-day window comes from this site’s verified Seasonal Events calendar. The Valentine Seasonal Event is the shortest celebration on the Core Keeper calendar, running only Feb 14 – Feb 17 — four days. Its currency works differently from every other event: instead of farming mob drops, you pick up Love Letters scattered on the ground around the world, then spend them at the Seasonal Merchant on a heart-themed crafting table, a storage chest and openable gifts.

item.title: Core Keeper World
item.description: World generation in Core Keeper is radial and deterministic. Every map is an underground layer that starts at The Core in the middle and spreads outward in rings; beyond a certain distance the plane is effectively endless. A hidden seed value baked into your save decides how those rings rotate, where each boss sits, and the exact shape of every chasm. Once you understand the ring layout, “where do I go next?

item.title: Core Keeper World Generation — Chunks, Seeds and Terrain Pipeline
item.description: World generation in Core Keeper is layered rather than instant. When you create a world, the game bakes a deterministic seed value into the save, but the map itself is not built all at once. Empty tiles start as solid Obsidian Blocks and only turn into dirt, stone, water and dungeons as players trigger them. This page explains the pipeline: what is fixed at creation, what is rolled as you explore, and why two players on the same seed always see the same map.
